Impassive describes a person who shows absolutely no emotion, no reaction, and no feeling — especially on their face or through their behavior. When someone is impassive, they look completely still and unreadable, like a blank wall, giving you no clue about what they think or feel about what is happening around them.

Picture this: you walk up to someone and tell them shocking news — say, that they just won a million dollars, or that their house is on fire. A normal person would react immediately — their eyes would widen, their mouth might drop open, they might gasp or jump up. But an impassive person? Nothing. No blink. No flinch. No change of expression whatsoever. They simply look back at you with a completely still, unreadable face.

Impassive works on two levels, and knowing both helps you understand it fully.

The first and more common layer is outward — what you can see on a person's face and body. The person may actually have feelings brewing inside them, but their face and body reveal absolutely none of it. A skilled poker player does this deliberately — they might feel excited or nervous, but their face stays impassive so no opponent can figure out their hand.

The second, deeper layer is inner — the person doesn't just hide their emotions, they genuinely don't feel anything in that moment. Their stillness isn't a mask; it's real emptiness inside.

When you encounter "impassive" in reading, it almost always refers to the first layer — the outward one. The person's appearance is what the word is describing.

Seeing a word used in context is one of the best ways to nail its meaning.

"Despite the crowd cheering around him, the soldier remained impassive, staring straight ahead." Here, everyone else is emotional, but the soldier shows nothing — no excitement, no pride, no irritation.

"She received the terrible news with an impassive expression — not a single tear, not even a frown." She heard something devastating but looked as though she'd heard nothing at all.

"The judge listened to both lawyers with an impassive face, giving nothing away." The judge showed neither agreement nor disagreement — a blank face throughout.

"His impassive stare made it impossible to know whether he was angry, bored, or simply thinking." You couldn't read him at all.

Notice how "impassive" almost always sits alongside a face, an expression, a stare, or a person in a moment of feeling — or rather, a moment of not visibly feeling.

This is important, because some words feel similar but are quite different.

Impassive does not mean the person is stupid or unaware. An impassive person may be deeply intelligent and paying close, careful attention — they just show nothing on the outside.

It does not mean the person is definitely emotionless inside. They could be feeling a hurricane of feelings — grief, joy, rage — but controlling what shows on their face.

It does not simply mean "calm." A calm person looks peaceful and at ease. An impassive person looks blank — like a face with all expression wiped completely clean. Calm is a feeling; impassive is an absence of visible feeling.

It does not mean unconscious, frozen, or in shock. An impassive person is fully present, fully awake, and functioning. They are simply choosing — or happen — to show nothing.

Impassive is a strong, absolute word. It doesn't describe someone who is a little less emotional than usual or who hides just a bit of what they feel. It means a complete absence of visible emotion — zero trace of any feeling showing through. If you want to say someone barely smiled, or seemed a little detached, impassive would be too strong. Impassive means nothing at all shows through.

Several words are close neighbors of impassive, but each has its own shade of meaning.

Expressionless is very similar, but it focuses only on the face. Impassive can describe a person's whole manner and bearing, not just their facial muscles.

Blank is also similar, but "blank" can suggest empty-mindedness or confusion (a "blank look" can mean someone didn't understand something). Impassive never implies confusion or stupidity — it is about the deliberate or natural absence of visible emotion, not lack of thought.

Stoic is related but carries a richer meaning. A stoic person deliberately endures pain, difficulty, or hardship without complaint, and they often look impassive because of that inner discipline. But "stoic" implies strength, willpower, and a conscious philosophy of endurance. "Impassive" is more neutral — it says nothing about strength or weakness, just that no emotion is showing.

Deadpan describes a deliberately flat, expressionless face — but almost always for humor. A comedian delivers a hilarious line with a completely straight face: that's deadpan. Impassive is broader and more serious, and has nothing to do with comedy.

Poker-faced is very close to impassive in meaning — hiding your feelings so others can't tell what you're thinking — but it is informal, comes from the card game of poker, and specifically implies a deliberate hiding of emotions. Impassive is more formal and literary, and doesn't always suggest it is deliberate.

Unemotional leans more toward the inner layer — actually not feeling much — whereas impassive leans more toward the outward layer of not showing emotion.
Antonyms — What Impassive Is the Opposite Of

Expressive — showing emotions openly and clearly through your face and body. The opposite of impassive.

Animated — full of lively movement and visible feeling. An animated face is always in motion, always reacting.

Demonstrative — freely showing feelings toward others, especially affection or enthusiasm.

Passionate — feeling and showing strong, intense emotion.
Connotation — Is It a Good Word or a Bad Word?

Impassive is neutral on its own — it is neither a compliment nor an insult by default. What it means in terms of tone depends entirely on the situation and context.

When used to describe a judge, a surgeon, or a soldier — people who should not let personal feelings get in the way of their work — impassive feels like a compliment. It suggests admirable professionalism, iron self-control, and fairness.

When used to describe a friend, a partner, or a parent in an emotional moment — someone who should show empathy and warmth — impassive feels cold, unsettling, or even cruel. It suggests a disturbing lack of connection.

When used in fiction to describe a villain or a mysterious character, impassive often creates a sense of unease or menace. We expect human beings to react to things. When someone doesn't, something feels deeply wrong about them — and authors use "impassive" to create exactly that eerie feeling.
How and Where Is It Typically Used?

Impassive is a formal, literary word. You will come across it far more in novels, serious journalism, and formal writing than in everyday casual conversation. In casual speech, people reach for phrases like "stone-faced," "poker face," "blank look," "straight face," or "he didn't even flinch" to express the same idea.

In writing, it almost always describes a person's face or expression, a person's reaction in a particular moment, or occasionally an entire crowd sitting in silence with no visible emotional response.
A Final Anchor to Lock It In

If one image could capture "impassive" perfectly, it's this: a stone statue of a human face. It has the shape of a face — the eyes, the mouth, the features — but it shows absolutely nothing. No joy, no sorrow, no surprise, no anger. Just still, blank, unreadable stone. When a person is described as impassive, that is exactly what they look like in that moment — a living human being whose face and manner have become, for now, as unreadable as stone.
